title: How I Built a SaaS in 30 Days

transcript.text: Thirty days ago this was an empty repo. Today it has paying customers, and I want to walk you through exactly how that happened.
I am going to cover four things: how I picked the problem, how I got the first users, how I priced it, and what I would do differently.
The problem came from my own workflow. I was doing the same manual task every week and I finally got annoyed enough to build something.
I want to be clear that I did not do customer discovery interviews. I was the customer. That is not always the right approach but it worked here.
So the build took about nine days for a version that did one thing. One thing, done properly, with no settings page.
That is the part people skip. They build six features badly instead of one feature well.

So going back to what I mentioned earlier about the agency, that whole period was really where the idea started forming, although at the time I did not think of it as a product at all, it was just a script I ran on Fridays.
Anyway. Distribution. This is the part that actually decides whether you have a business.

My first 40 customers came from a spreadsheet, not ads. I opened a blank sheet, listed 200 companies that had publicly complained about the exact problem I solved, and sent 200 emails that each referenced their own words back to them.
The reply rate was about 19 percent, which is absurd, and it is absurd because the emails were not cold. They were specific.
I did try paid ads for a week. I spent 400 dollars and got two signups, both of which churned. So I stopped.
Let us talk about pricing, because this is where I made the biggest mistake and then the biggest correction.

I tripled my price and lost exactly zero customers. Here is the thing nobody tells you about pricing early: your first ten customers are not buying software, they are buying a fix for a problem that is costing them more than your price tag.
I started at nineteen dollars because that felt safe. It was not safe. It signalled that the thing was a toy.
When I moved to fifty nine, the conversations changed. People asked about onboarding instead of asking whether it was free.
I wake up at 5:30 and I do not check my phone for the first hour, which honestly is the thing everybody says, but for me it genuinely did change how the first block of work went.
Right, back to the product. The onboarding was three screens and I cut it to one.
Support was me, in a shared inbox, for the entire first month. That is not scalable and I would not defend it, but it taught me the objections faster than any survey would have.
Distribution is not a channel, it is a compounding loop. Every customer you land should make the next one cheaper to reach. If it does not, you do not have distribution, you have advertising.
The loop for me was simple: every customer got a shareable output with a small footer, and that footer drove about a third of new signups by week four.
I want to flag that this works for tools with a visible output. If your product is invisible, you need a different loop, probably content.
Okay, two more things and then I will wrap up, because I know this is getting long.

Quick word from today's sponsor before we get into the last part. If you have ever tried to set up analytics for a side project you know how long that takes, and this is the tool I actually use for it.
Last thing. What I would do differently. I would price higher on day one, and I would start the outreach spreadsheet before the product was finished.
